title: HTML Editors
summary: Set up a free code editor, create an HTML file the right way, open it in a browser and use developer tools to inspect any page.
introduction: You can write HTML in any plain-text editor, but a code editor makes the job far more pleasant: it colours your tags, closes them for you and shows mistakes as you type. This lesson sets up Visual Studio Code, creates a project folder, saves a page with the correct file extension and introduces the browser developer tools you will rely on for the rest of your career.
learningObjectives: Install and configure a code editor for HTML work
Create, save and open an HTML file with the correct extension
Use View Source and Inspect to look at any page's HTML

blocks.text: Any of these works well; pick one and stay with it while you learn.

rows: Syntax colouring, auto-closing tags, a huge extension library and a built-in terminal. Used in this tutorial.
Very fast and lightweight, good for quick edits.
Full IDE with refactoring and debugging built in.
Minimal, but still colours HTML and is better than Notepad.

blocks.title: Avoid word processors
blocks.text: Do not write HTML in Microsoft Word or Google Docs. They add hidden formatting and save files that browsers cannot read as HTML.

items: Download VS Code from [code.visualstudio.com](https://code.visualstudio.com) and install it.
Create a folder for your projects, for example `my-website`, and open it with **File → Open Folder**.
Create a new file with **File → New File** and save it as `index.html`. The `.html` extension is what tells the editor and the browser that the file contains HTML.
Optional but useful: install the **Live Server** extension so the browser reloads automatically whenever you save.

blocks.text: Type `!` and press **Tab** in an empty `.html` file. VS Code expands it into a complete starting document, which is a handy way to avoid typos in the boilerplate.

blocks.title: What the ! shortcut produces
blocks.code:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
  <meta charset="UTF-8">
  <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1.0">
  <title>Document</title>
</head>
<body>

</body>
</html>

blocks.text: The `viewport` meta tag is new compared with the previous lesson. It tells phones to render the page at the device width instead of pretending to be a desktop screen; you will want it on every page you build.
Opening the page in a browser

Double-click `index.html` in your file manager, or drag it onto a browser window. The address bar shows a `file://` path, which simply means the page is loaded from your disk. Every time you change the file, save it and press **F5** (or **Ctrl+R**) to reload.

If the browser shows your HTML tags as plain text, the file was probably saved as `index.html.txt` or `index.txt`. Check the extension; on Windows enable "File name extensions" in Explorer so you can see it.
Browsers let you see the HTML behind every page, which is one of the best ways to learn. Two tools matter:

items: **View Source** (`Ctrl+U` in Chrome, Edge and Firefox) shows the exact HTML the server sent.
**Inspect** (right-click any element → *Inspect*, or press `F12`) opens the developer tools, where you see the live document tree, can edit it temporarily and see which CSS applies.

blocks.title: Habit worth building
blocks.text: When you see a layout or component you like on any site, inspect it. Reading real HTML written by other developers teaches patterns no tutorial can cover completely.
Keep the following structure as you work through the lessons. It mirrors how real projects separate pages, styles, scripts and images.

blocks.title: Folder layout
blocks.code:
my-website/
├── index.html
├── about.html
├── css/
│   └── styles.css
├── js/
│   └── main.js
└── images/
    └── logo.png
